newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Albright hails Czechs as democrats, ready for NATO.
newsitem.headline: Albright hails Czechs as democrats, ready for NATO.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, on an emotional visit to her native Prague, said on Monday she was confident the Czech Republic would do everything necessary to be ready for NATO membership in 1999.

Albright, speaking after NATO last week invited the Czech Republic, Poland and Hungary to apply to join the alliance, told Czechs they were resuming their rightful place among European democracies "fully, finally and forever".
At a news conference, she said Czech leaders understood that first-class NATO membership would require a first-class contribution.

"I am confident that the Czech Republic is ready to take the responsibility as a mature democracy for the wellbeing and security of others," she told a news conference after talks with President Vaclav Havel and other Czech leaders.

Albright said the Czechs would have to streamline and modernise their armed forces and that by 2000 they should be spending two percent of gross domestic product on defence. The figure is currently about 1.7 percent.

In the single controversial note of an otherwise triumphal visit, Albright said the United States also expected the Czechs to tighten up their laws on exports to "rogue states" -- an apparent reference to alleged arms sales to Iran and Iraq.

Karel Kovanda, a Czech deputy foreign minister responsible for arms exports, told reporters his office would not sanction such sales. "We are looking for documentation so we can stamp this out," he said.

Albright's visit was shot through with exultation that the land of her birth had emerged from 50 years of Nazi and communist oppression to qualify for membership in NATO and other Western institutions.

"Nothing compares to the feeling of coming to my original home, Prague, as the Secretary of State of the United States, for the purpose of saying to you: Welcome home," she said in an impassioned speech in Prague's art nouveau municipal hall.
Albright predicted that the U.S. Senate would approve NATO expansion but said the "burden of proof will still rest with those of us who believe that NATO enlargement serves American interests".

She dismissed as a "tired myth" the argument "that in times of crisis we will make no sacrifice to defend a distant city with an unpronounceable name: that we will protect the freedom of Barcelona but not Brno, Stuttgart but not Szczecin."

In her news conference and speech, Albright commiserated over severe floods which have hit the north and east of the Czech Republic in the past week. She said the U.S. government had offered help and added, "That is what friends are for."
Albright, who was born in Prague in 1937 and speaks Czech, was unhappy with some of the translation of her news conference remarks.

"Not exactly," she said after a tribute to Havel, the former anti-communist dissident who rose to become president, had not been translated as she wished. After repeating the phrase in English, she then delivered her own Czech version.
She later corrected another phrase and eventually the humilated interpreter stood aside and allowed Havel's personal interpreter to translate the rest of the news conference.

Albright's first visit to Prague since taking on her post in January began on an emotional note on Sunday. She visited Prague's Jewish quarter and saw the names of her paternal grandparents on the memorial walls of a synagogue dedicated to some 80,000 Czechoslovak Jews who died in the Holocaust.
Albright, who says she only recently became aware of her Jewish origins, said the image of the names "will forever be seared into my heart".
Albright, whose family twice fled the former Czechoslovakia, met her only known relative in the Czech Republic, cousin Dagmar Simova, in her hotel on Monday.
Simova's husband, Vladimir Sima, confirmed they had met but declined to say what was discussed.

Prague has long seen Albright as a powerful friend and supporter of their NATO membership. But Havel said Czech origin by itself "does not guarantee anything" and it was her "fine feeling for European problems" for which he esteemed her.

In a stay of less than 24 hours in Prague before returning to Washington, Albright received the Czechs' highest civilian award, the Order of the White Lion, "for especially outstanding endeavour to the benefit of the Czech Republic".
